title: Tongues, Love, and Perfect Knowledge
english: …to the unworthy for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love belongs to the devout. So this is what he says: “Earnestly desire the greater gifts. And I am showing you a way” (1 Corinthians 12:31) that leads you to the enjoyment of the greater gifts, and the way is love. The one who loves fulfills the law; the one who fulfills the law wins approval; the one who wins approval receives a spiritual gift.
The second catena form adds: He saw them envying those who had the gifts while their love stayed cold, so he teaches that love is the highest good of all.

On 1 Corinthians 13:1: And what tongue do angels have, when they have no chest, no larynx, no tongue, no voice? But Moses says in Deuteronomy that God set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God (Deuteronomy 32:8). He clearly set them at the time when he divided into languages those who had tried to build the tower. They were no longer kept in concord by a common speech; they had become strangers to one another, as it were, through the changes of language. So angels were appointed, each to guard the nation entrusted to him, so that none might be squandered and lost. That is why he calls the difference of languages “tongues of angels.” We should know that, just as David speaks of “bread of angels” (Psalm 78:25) not because angels eat, so he speaks of “tongues of angels” not because angels speak. Both are said because the angels serve God's ordering of things. The “tongue of men,” then, is the trained tongue, for the artful tongue is something brought in on top of the natural one. The “tongue of angels” is the natural tongue divided into many. “I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” From this it is clear that by “of angels” he means the change and difference of languages. Someone who speaks in other tongues among people who do not know them is like a cymbal that makes only a noise and shows no meaning.
The second catena form adds: By “tongue of men” he means the language of rhetoric, grammar, philosophy, speculation, prose writing, the arts and debate.

On 1 Corinthians 13:2: By “mystery” he means anything that is unknown but revealed by the power of the Spirit. Each such thing is a mystery, as he says elsewhere, “For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery” (Romans 11:25), and again, “Look, I tell you a mystery” (1 Corinthians 15:51).

On 1 Corinthians 13:4: A little further on he teaches what love is, where he says, “Love is patient,” and the rest. So showing mercy is one thing and loving is another. Even giving one's property to the poor and handing oneself over to martyrdom, if it is not yet done for love's sake, slips without our noticing into vainglory and empty ambition. So if we share, we must share out of love for the one who receives or out of love for God who commanded it; and if we bear witness, we must endure it out of love for the Lord.
On 1 Corinthians 13:8: “Love never fails”: that is, it never slips into sin.
On 1 Corinthians 13:10: What is partial is done away with when complete knowledge has been given. We know little now, and more still lies hidden.

On 1 Corinthians 13:11–12: When I was a child, he says, I had a child's way of reasoning, but when I grew to full manhood I had a man's understanding. I no longer knew simply that my father is my father, but also in what sense he is a father. In the same way, whatever I know in part now, I will learn at the time of completion; and what I grasp now only dimly, as in a mirror, I will then know clearly. He did not say, “Then I will know mysteries,” which would have been the natural sequel, but “I will be known.” The one who is known by God and made his own is the one who also gains the sight of the mysteries with his own eyes.
On 1 Corinthians 13:13: Since not all knowledge has yet been revealed to us, what remains for us is to believe that all knowledge will be revealed to us.

added_allusions.reason: Lemma quoted: ποθεῖτε τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ κρείττονα. καὶ ὁδὸν ὑμῖν δείκνυμι.
Quoted in Septuagint wording: ἔστησεν ὅρια ἐθνῶν κατὰ ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ (the Hebrew/KJV has 'children of Israel').
Quoted: οὐ γὰρ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο.
'the one who loves fulfills the law' (ὁ γὰρ ἀγαπῶν νόμον πληροῖ) echoes Romans 13:8; not cited inline because Severianus builds it into his own chain.
Division of languages at the tower; alluded to, not quoted.

title: The distinction between tongues and prophecy
english: And believers believe so that they may hope, and those who hope need love, so that we do not fall away from hope. That is why he said, “Greater than this is love,” for it is through love that the law is fulfilled.

On 1 Corinthians 14:1–5: If he does not interpret, but only speaks in a tongue and does not make its meaning clear, because he lacks this gift of interpretation, he does speak mysteries (that is, clearly, the Spirit who supplies the tongues does) and he utters mysteries through the tongues. But he does not build up the church, which does not understand what he is saying. The one who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, knowing that he is uttering what he did not know; he perceived that the grace of the Holy Spirit was in him, and he was built up. So if the one who speaks in tongues also interprets, he is not less than the prophet.

“Be eager,” he says, “for prophecy more than the other gifts.” He said this because the gifts were given to match each person's way of life, and it was up to them which gift they wished to be eager for and receive. When some speak in tongues, no one who hears understands. Even so, though what is spoken is unclear to people, the one who speaks in the Spirit speaks mysteries (for the Spirit who supplies the tongues utters mysteries), while the one who prophesies helps those who hear, because he speaks to them plainly. The grace is greater if the one who speaks in tongues also receives the gift of interpreting; perhaps it was that he did not have both.

On 1 Corinthians 14:6: What good will I do you, he says, if I cannot speak to you about what was revealed to me by God, or about what I myself have come to know and grasp, or about what I have understood in the prophets, or about what I have resolved to counsel or teach you? If I speak about these things and you do not understand, what good will I do you?
On 1 Corinthians 14:7: Consider, he says, that even with lifeless things, the flute and the lyre, if the notes are not distinct, what is piped or played becomes a blur.
On 1 Corinthians 14:10: “Nothing is without voice”: that is, clearly, no race of men.
On 1 Corinthians 14:12: By “spiritual things” he means the different gifts of the Holy Spirit.

On 1 Corinthians 14:13–14: If, he says, I speak in some tongue that I do not know, without even knowing what it means, I am persuaded that my mind is unfruitful, since it does not have the meaning of what was said. Let him pray to obtain a double grace: to speak in tongues and to interpret them. Praying in a tongue is the working of the Holy Spirit, but the mind bears no fruit, because no one can understand what is said or benefit from it. That is why, he says, I must do this: make clear what the Spirit supplies to me, to build up those who hear, so that my mind is not unfruitful for want of the meaning of the words.

On 1 Corinthians 14:16: Because no one can benefit from what is said or understand it, if I give thanks in a tongue, the listener does not give you back the “Amen.” By “outsider” he means one who, so to speak, has not yet enlisted: one not yet baptized.
On 1 Corinthians 14:19: With the clarity of the mind, and in the ordinary language.
On 1 Corinthians 14:20: Be eager to become mature: to understand the Scriptures.

On 1 Corinthians 14:21–23: Note this. When the Jews are asked to show where God spoke to them in many tongues and they disobeyed, they cannot show it. But we show that when the Holy Spirit came and made the division into tongues, the Jews in their disbelief said, “They are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13). So tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, and prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. Tongues do build up, then, when the hearer learns that the speaker is speaking a language he does not know; yet he does not receive the building up that comes from the benefit of spiritual teaching, since it is not understood and makes no headway. Prophecy concerns things to come, and it is not just anyone who believes what is said about them, but the believer. The unbeliever needs a man who does not know the language he is using, and who so shows that the Spirit of God is in him. So the tongue was a wonder, while prophecy was a wonder by its fulfillment, not in the speaking. Divine Scripture speaks of unbelief in two ways: the true unbelief of the Greeks, and the little faith of the devout. By “unbeliever” he means the Greek, and by “outsider” the one not yet baptized, the one not yet enlisted; at that time they were not called catechumens or unbaptized.

The second catena form adds: He calls the writings of the other prophets “law” too, since they lived under the law. What was spoken through Isaiah (Isaiah 28:11) came to pass when the Spirit came down on the apostles and they spoke in tongues and the Jews mocked. Clearly tongues are of benefit when the hearer realizes that the speaker is speaking a language he does not know and did not learn from men. Yet the thing does not benefit the…

'through love the law is fulfilled' echoes Romans 13:10; not cited inline because it is Severianus's own sentence.

title: The Necessity of the Resurrection
english: …hearer, because it is not understood. The sign is given to unbelievers, so that they may believe what they see; prophecy is given so that one may accept what was said and bless the Lord.
On 1 Corinthians 14:26: Let each one build up the church through whatever grace he has from God.

On 1 Corinthians 14:28: By saying “let him be silent,” he taught that one who speaks by the Holy Spirit speaks when he wishes and keeps silent when he wishes, as the prophets did. Not so those possessed by an unclean spirit: they speak even when they do not wish to, and say things they do not know.

On 1 Corinthians 14:29–32: By these words he shows that the Holy Spirit revealed the mysteries to souls, and they, once enlightened, revealed them to men. It was not as in soothsaying, where the soothsayer does not know what he is uttering. So he has now made good what he said at the start: that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to the dumb idols, carried off as you were. “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge”: those who have the gift of discerning spirits. “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent,” since it lies with them at one time to be silent and at another to speak. “And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.” Do not be afraid, he says, that by falling silent you are slighting the Spirit, for the gifts know how to yield to one another.
The second catena form adds that this is so that the church may be built up and there may be no confusion from everyone speaking at once.

On 1 Corinthians 15:1–2: I am not telling you anything strange, he says, but what I preached. And it is not that I preached and you did not accept it: you received it. Nor did you receive something empty and useless, but that in which you are being saved. Since he is about to say, “I made known to you how the Lord Jesus died for us,” he says, “in what word”: this gospel, given so that the resurrection may be believed, for Jesus, who died for us, is the firstfruits of the resurrection. If death did not have to be destroyed, the Savior would not have become man. “Unless you believed in vain” stands for “except if you believed in vain.” For I say that if you do not hold it fast, it is plain that you believed in vain.

On 1 Corinthians 15:3: He said “first of all” meaning “before everything else”: I handed this on to you. I did not hand on an argument of my own, but what I received from the Scriptures. It was confirmed to him by his own eyes that Christ died and rose, and Christ called him from heaven.
On 1 Corinthians 15:4: How was he buried, if, as the heretics say, he did not have flesh?
On 1 Corinthians 15:6: “Above five hundred” means “more than five hundred.”

On 1 Corinthians 15:8: An untimely birth is what is expelled from the womb before it has been fully formed and has had its proper time there, and it cannot live. Just as babies are shaped in the womb, souls were shaped beforehand under the law toward godliness, and were born again of water and Spirit (John 3:5). Paul, though, persecuted the church without being shaped to completion under the law; he was persecuting it. That is why he called himself an untimely birth, and he adds next, “because I persecuted the church of God.”

On 1 Corinthians 15:9–10a: “The least of the apostles,” because they did not persecute but believed, while I persecuted. He was a persecutor, and yet by God's foreknowledge he obtained so great a grace; that is why he also labored more than the others.
On 1 Corinthians 15:10b: I did not receive great grace for nothing. I used it for the preaching, and labored more abundantly than all of them.
On 1 Corinthians 15:12–13: It cannot be that Christ rose and the rest do not. It is agreed that Christ died and rose for no other reason than our resurrection.
On 1 Corinthians 15:14–18: If Christ has not been raised, he says, in vain…
